[Graph: $c$ / cm s$^{-1}$ (0–20) against $d$ / cm (0–15); data points with vertical error bars rising from about 5.5 at d = 2.5 to about 18.5 at d = 16, curving; the point at d = 15 cm (c ≈ 18) has no error bar]

(ii) On the graph opposite, draw the error bar for the data point corresponding to $d = 15$ cm. [1]
(b) Caroline hypothesized that the wave speed $c$ is directly proportional to the water depth $d$.
(i) On the graph opposite, draw a line of best-fit for the data. [1]
(ii) Suggest if the data support this hypothesis. [2]

questions.text:
A2. This question is about internal energy.
Humans generate internal energy when moving, while their core temperature remains
approximately constant.
(a)  Distinguish between the concepts of internal energy and temperature.  [3]
(b)  Explain, in terms of molecular behaviour, how the evaporation of sweat enables humans
to maintain a constant temperature.  [3]

A4. This question is about escape speed and gravitational effects.
(a)  Explain what is meant by escape speed.  [2]
(b)  Titania is a moon that orbits the planet Uranus.  The mass of Titania is 3.5×1021 kg.
The radius of Titania is 800 km.
(i)  Use the data to calculate the gravitational potential at the surface of Titania.  [2]
(ii)  Use your answer to (b)(i) to determine the escape speed for Titania.  [3]
(c)  An astronaut visiting Titania throws an object away from him with an initial horizontal
velocity of 1.8 m s–1.  The object is 1.5 m above the moon’s surface when it is thrown.
The gravitational field strength at the surface of Titania is 0.37 N kg–1.
Calculate the distance from the astronaut at which the object first strikes the surface.  [3]

An isolated nucleus of an atom of the metal tungsten contains 74 protons.
[Diagram: nucleus at centre of a circle; point X on the circle]
Point X is 140 pm from the nucleus.
(a) (i) On the diagram above, draw an arrow to show the direction of the electric field at point X. [1]
(ii) Assuming the nucleus acts as a point charge, determine the magnitude of the electric field strength at point X. [2]
(b) Tungsten is a conductor used as the filament of an electric lamp. The filament of the lamp is surrounded by glass which is an insulator.
Outline, in terms of their atomic structure, the difference between the electrical properties of tungsten and of glass. [2]
(c) A tungsten filament lamp is marked 6.0 V, 15 W.
(i) Show that the resistance of the lamp at its working voltage is 2.4 Ω. [1]
(ii) The length of the filament is 0.35 m and the resistivity of tungsten is $5.6\times10^{-7}$ Ω m at its working voltage.
Calculate the cross-sectional area of the tungsten filament. [2]
(d) The diagram shows part of a potential divider circuit used to measure the current-potential difference ($I$–$V$) characteristic of the bulb.
[Circuit: 6 V battery connected across a potentiometer with a sliding contact]
(i) Draw the complete circuit showing the correct position of the bulb, ammeter and voltmeter. [2]
(ii) On the axes provided, sketch a graph to show how the current in the bulb varies with the potential difference. [2]
[Axes: current against potential difference]
(e) A student sets up a different circuit to measure the $I$–$V$ graph. The cell has an emf of 6.0 V and negligible internal resistance. The variable resistor has a minimum resistance of zero and a maximum resistance of 5.0 Ω.
[Circuit: 6.0 V cell in series with a lamp and a variable resistor 0–5.0 Ω]
Explain, with a calculation, why this circuit will not allow for a full range of potential difference from 0 V to 6 V across the bulb. Assume that the resistance of the lamp remains constant at a value of 2.4 Ω. [3]
Part 2 Properties of a gas
A fixed mass of an ideal gas is at an initial volume of $2.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$. It undergoes an adiabatic expansion to a volume of $5.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$. An identical ideal gas undergoes the same change of volume but this time isothermally.
The graph shows the variation with volume $V$ of the pressure $P$ of the two gases.
[Graph: $P$ / $\times10^5$ Pa (2–8) against $V$ / $\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$ (2.0–5.0); gas B curve starts at about 7.2, gas A curve starts at 5.0; both end at about 2.0 at V = 5.0]
(a) Using data from the graph above, identify which gas, A or B, undergoes the isothermal expansion. [2]
(b) Using the graph opposite, estimate the difference in work done by each gas. [4]
(c) Explain, with reference to the first law of thermodynamics, and without further calculation, the change in temperature of the gas undergoing the adiabatic change. [4]
